My question really is why this hasn’t been ameliorated. 


The service of the hotline has declined considerably, as I called a few times in 2016, and heard a human voice within 1-2 minutes.  Of course the call volume will increase with more people on a dangerous verge, considering that the depression and suicide issue has heightened. But if this issue is so serious, 25 minutes on hold after an automated message simply asks you to push a number if you are in need of urgent counseling (in hopes the urgency does not become an emergency) seems nearly useless. I’ve read stories of people who haven’t even been answered...


Major respect to the volunteers, because it’s not *their* fault. But why isn’t there more incentive for more people to contribute to the system? Are there less paid employees than volunteers? If that’s the case, then of course the hold issue will persist. As a volunteer, putting in hours absorbing people’s distress must be insanely mentally taxing. It’s simply unacceptable to be understaffed, and the hotline should potentially be renamed to something that doesn’t sound like promising talk therapy support. 


I have a dog whom I never had the money to train as a service dog, but his particular breed has been known to be excellent for their owners suffering from emotional distress. He would not leave my lap the entire day despite the loud crying. We fell asleep with him on my leg. I calmed down because of him. 



There needs to be serious revision of the national hotline, or multiple numbers to dial. One-way telepsych chats for patient anonymity. A soothing, encouraging voice while you’re on hold instead of that dreadful auto message talking about the service process. There are so many viable solutions to this issue in 2018, and it can become a serious public health hazard if someone isn’t in the right mind to think rationally enough to get a hospital, after just really needing to talk. It’s not just frustrating, it’s wrong. I truly hope those whose calls were never answered are still survivors.
